title: A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a decisive account of how secure standardized lattice-based key establishment is against quantum computation. Its immediate target is ML-KEM, a mechanism that lets two parties establish a shared secret for subsequent symmetric-key cryptography. The desired advance would be either a consequential, fully specified quantum attack or a concrete security guarantee backed by an applicable quantum lower bound. Neither outcome is presented here as achieved.

Three mathematical layers must remain distinct. Plain learning with errors, or LWE, involves recovering information from noisy linear relations. Module LWE introduces algebraic structure and is the presumed hard problem underlying ML-KEM. The complete ML-KEM construction adds cryptographic transformations intended to protect key establishment against chosen-ciphertext attacks. A result about plain LWE therefore does not automatically settle the security of structured module LWE or of the complete standardized mechanism.

Scope synthesis: ML-KEM-512 is the proposed first target, while the retained title describes a broader ambition. Resolving that parameter set would be a major milestone, but would not by itself classify ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024, or all deployed lattice encryption. The proposed attack and security milestones are also not exhaustive alternatives: an eventual result could establish security or insecurity at resource levels between their thresholds.

significance.text: ML-KEM is an approved post-quantum key-establishment mechanism whose security rests on presumed module-LWE hardness. A successful quantum attack recovering its established shared secret would undermine the secrecy of systems relying on that mechanism alone under the attack's stated conditions. This would affect a concrete cryptographic capability, rather than merely improve an abstract lattice algorithm.

Impact synthesis: the consequences of an ML-KEM-512 attack would depend on its mechanism. An attack exploiting a broadly shared mathematical weakness could threaten larger ML-KEM parameter sets or other lattice constructions. An attack specific to one parameter set or transformation might have much narrower reach. Effects on lattice signatures, homomorphic encryption, and other lattice-based systems would require separate applicability arguments; retirement of the entire lattice public-key stack does not follow from a single-set break. The supplied evidence also does not establish deployment prevalence or ML-KEM's primacy relative to other standards.

A security result could be equally consequential if it connected the actual standardized parameters to a quantitative lower bound against general quantum computation. Existing reductions explain how an efficient solver for one problem would yield a solver for another; they do not independently prove that either problem requires large resources. FIPS 203 already records asymptotic theoretical security in a heuristic model, alongside concrete security strengths estimated from cryptanalysis. The proposed advance would have to strengthen that existing foundation in a precisely stated way.

This goal does not require proving NP-hardness. Peikert's report documents barriers for specified lattice approximation problems, norms, and approximation factors: their membership in classes such as coAM or coNP would make appropriate NP-hardness claims imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. These qualifications matter; the report does not establish an unrestricted barrier for every lattice problem or directly classify a fixed ML-KEM instance.

Scope synthesis: smaller keys and faster operations could improve ML-KEM's practical use, but they answer a different question from establishing its quantum security or demonstrating a consequential attack. The revolutionary claim here concerns the strength of the security conclusion, not routine implementation efficiency.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a concrete bridge from the mathematics of lattice problems to a decisive quantum resource statement about standardized ML-KEM. Regev's quantum worst-case connection, independently described in Peikert's report, relates suitable plain-LWE instances to worst-case problems including GapSVP and SIVP. Its applicability depends on approximation factors and noise conditions. It transfers algorithmic consequences between problems; it does not establish an unconditional quantum lower bound, and it does not automatically cover ML-KEM's module structure and full construction.

Attack-side proposal: the breakthrough would require an explicit quantum procedure that succeeds on the standardized key and encapsulation distributions, with a correctness argument and a credible accounting of its resources. A favorable asymptotic expression alone would leave open whether constants, memory, preprocessing, or access assumptions make the attack relevant to ML-KEM-512. Conversely, a fixed sub-2^80-gate attack would not necessarily be a polynomial-time algorithm; concrete cost and asymptotic complexity are different claims.

Security-side proposal: the engineering and mathematical challenge is to make every link quantitative. A theorem must cover the complete ML-KEM construction, its assumptions and adversarial access model, the losses incurred by the reduction, and the standardized dimensions, moduli, and distributions. It must then connect to a lower bound strong enough to imply the claimed security level. A lower bound in a restricted model remains restricted even if that model permits hidden-subgroup period-finding. General quantum security requires coverage of general quantum computation.

The supplied evidence establishes the motivation and historical foundations, but does not establish whether either proposed breakthrough remained absent on 1 November 2026. There is no supplied freshness-search record supporting a comprehensive claim about public attacks or security theorems through that date.

current_state.text: FIPS 203 was published and became effective on 13 August 2024. It specifies ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024, and describes ML-KEM as believed secure against adversaries possessing quantum computers. Its account is more specific than a simple assertion that security is unproved: it records asymptotic theoretical security in a heuristic model, while concrete security strengths are estimated from cryptanalysis. These are meaningful existing results, but neither supplies the unconditional concrete quantum guarantee envisioned here.

Regev's historical result provides a quantum connection between suitable plain-LWE instances and worst-case GapSVP and SIVP. Peikert's report, dated 3 December 2006, independently describes that connection and establishes limits on NP-hardness for specified lattice approximation problems and factors. These results support the distinction between conditional hardness, reductions, and lower bounds; they do not themselves resolve the security of the standardized ML-KEM parameter sets.

The supplied review had access to the relevant FIPS 203 security discussion, but the retained PDF extraction ends in Appendix C. The landing page is also not a substitute for the complete specification. These limitations do not prevent use of the reviewed security passages, but they limit claims about material beyond them. The supplied research additionally reports a planning note dated 17 November 2025 concerning an erratum; that report should not be interpreted as evidence of a cryptanalytic break.

The saved INSPIRE extraction contained only the site name, so the supplied review could not verify the attributed document identity or abstract quotations from that artifact. This is an access limitation, not evidence that Regev's result is false. The historical connection described above instead relies on the independently reviewed Peikert report.

Evidence boundary: retrieval of the supplied materials on 1 November 2026 does not establish a literature survey through that date. Accordingly, the record cannot confirm the earlier claims that no public quantum polynomial-time break exists, that no applicable hardness argument exists, or that the proposed classification remains open in both directions. No achieved attack or conclusive security theorem is established by the supplied evidence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attack milestone: provide a fully specified quantum algorithm and correctness proof that recover the shared secret from an honestly generated ML-KEM-512 encapsulation using public information, with success probability at least two-thirds and fewer than 2^80 quantum gates. Specify a universal gate set and account explicitly for classical computation, memory, preprocessing, and all access assumptions. The probability and gate thresholds are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards or reported achievements.
completion_criteria.label: Recover ML-KEM-512 secrets with ≥⅔ success using <2^80 quantum gates

completion_criteria.text: Proposed security milestone: provide a concrete theorem showing how a specified IND-CCA advantage against ML-KEM-512 yields an algorithm for a named worst-case lattice problem, with explicit losses and assumptions covering the standardized construction and parameters. Pair it with a quantitative lower bound in the same computational model that is sufficient for the claimed security level. FIPS 203's discussion of chosen-ciphertext security motivates this target; it does not endorse these proposed completion conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Establish ML-KEM-512 security via reduction and sufficient quantum lower bounds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation rule: identify exactly what the theorem establishes. A reduction without a lower bound remains conditional on the hardness of its target problem. A lower bound for a restricted class of quantum algorithms establishes security only against that class, even when it includes period-finding. Absence of known attacks is insufficient for the security milestone, and a concrete attack below a fixed gate threshold does not by itself establish a polynomial-time break.
completion_criteria.label: State exactly the theorem’s security scope and hardness assumptions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: publish enough algorithmic, mathematical, and resource-estimation detail for independent researchers to reproduce the analysis and check the claimed advantage. Attack demonstrations should distinguish success on honestly generated standardized instances from success on specially selected examples. Security claims should expose all reduction losses and model assumptions to independent scrutiny. Experiments can substantiate performance and success rates, but cannot replace the proof required by either proposed milestone.
completion_criteria.label: Publish independently reproducible analyses supporting claimed advantages and required proofs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: report separately the implications for ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024, and any other construction. State whether attack costs concern abstract logical gates or an implemented machine and make the relationship explicit. Finite testing establishes demonstrated breadth across the tested instances, not literal universality. Neither proposed milestone should be advertised as an exhaustive classification of lattice cryptography without additional results covering the wider scope.
completion_criteria.label: Report parameter-specific ML-KEM implications, cost models, and scope limits

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis — CRY-01, A proof that an explicit one-way function exists: both concepts seek firmer foundations for cryptographic hardness. CRY-01 concerns a foundational existence claim, whereas CRY-10 concerns quantum security and concrete resources for a specified key-establishment construction. A conditional ML-KEM reduction does not by itself prove the existence of an unconditionally hard one-way function.

Roster synthesis — CRY-02, Public-key encryption from one-way functions: both concern foundations for public-key capabilities. CRY-02 asks whether a weaker primitive suffices to construct public-key encryption; CRY-10 asks how secure an existing standardized lattice mechanism is against quantum computation. Neither question resolves the other automatically.

Roster synthesis — CRY-03, Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation: a quantum attack or security theorem for a relevant lattice assumption could inform an obfuscation construction using that assumption. Such a connection would require matching problems and parameters. Establishing ML-KEM security would not establish practical obfuscation, and an ML-KEM-specific break would not automatically defeat it.

Roster synthesis — CRY-04, General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost: private-computation systems may depend on lattice-based components, including homomorphic encryption. CRY-10 could affect confidence in those components if its result extends to their assumptions. It does not address their computation overhead, and an ML-KEM-512 break alone would not establish a break of homomorphic encryption.

Roster synthesis — CRY-05, Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs: both involve security against quantum adversaries. CRY-05 additionally concerns quantum states, verification, and resistance to copying; CRY-10 concerns the computational security of a classical key-establishment mechanism. Any dependence through shared assumptions would need to be demonstrated.

Roster synthesis — CRY-06, Practical classical verification of quantum computation: verification methods could help assess an implemented quantum computation relevant to an attack. They would not substitute for the attack's correctness and resource analysis, nor establish a lower bound excluding other quantum algorithms. CRY-06 concerns checking computations; CRY-10 concerns the limits and consequences of adversarial computation.

Roster synthesis — CRY-07, Position verification that works in physical spacetime: both require precise adversarial models, but CRY-07 centers on location, timing, and physical constraints. CRY-10 centers on computational hardness. A lattice-security theorem would not resolve the physical and coordination assumptions of position verification.

Roster synthesis — CRY-08, Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost: secure key establishment can support confidential messaging, but concealing message contents does not conceal communication patterns. CRY-10 could strengthen or undermine a messaging system's key-establishment component without resolving metadata privacy or its cost.

Roster synthesis — CRY-09, Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem: both seek rigorous constraints on quantum adversaries. CRY-09 requires a statement about unavoidable sequential work and release timing; CRY-10 seeks attack or security bounds for ML-KEM. A total-resource hardness result does not automatically imply sequentiality, and a sequentiality theorem does not classify ML-KEM.

brief.title: Knowing how safe shared secrets are from quantum computers
possible: People protecting private communications could choose encryption with a decisive account of its quantum security: a quantified guarantee or a fully specified attack. The initial target would be ML-KEM-512, a standardized way for people to agree on a secret encryption key.
why: An attack that recovered the shared secret would undermine privacy in systems relying on this mechanism alone. A security guarantee would give system designers a firmer mathematical basis for trusting it against quantum computers.

sources.who: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.showed: The organisation standardized ML-KEM for establishing shared secret keys. It relates security to the difficulty of solving structured equations with deliberately added noise.
sources.quote: This standard specifies a key-encapsulation mechanism called ML-KEM.
sources.cited_for: The standard defines the mechanism whose quantum security would have to be settled.
sources.not_established: The standard does not establish the proposed concrete guarantee against general quantum computation.

sources.showed: Peikert proved limits on claims of mathematical difficulty for certain problems on lattices, repeating grids of points, under different ways of measuring distance.
sources.quote:
Approximating the shortest and closest vector in the 𝓁p norm to within ˜O(√n) factors is
contained in coNP.
sources.cited_for: The work clarifies limits on hardness claims for mathematical problems underlying lattice cryptography.
sources.not_established: These results neither break ML-KEM nor prove how much quantum computation attacking it requires.

shown: The National Institute of Standards and Technology has standardized ML-KEM. Its security foundation includes theoretical arguments in an idealized model and strength estimates based on studying attacks. Existing mathematical connections transfer difficulty between problems without proving a minimum quantum attack cost.
missing: A fully specified quantum attack meeting the proposed success and cost requirements on normally generated secrets is needed.
A quantitative proof must connect the complete standardized mechanism to a mathematical problem with a sufficient quantum cost lower bound.
The mathematical guarantees must cover ML-KEM’s structured equations and full construction, rather than simpler related problems.

milestones.label: Secret recovery below the proposed quantum cost ceiling
milestones.explanation: An attack would have to recover normally generated shared secrets from public data with the required success rate using fewer than 2^80 quantum gates, or basic operations. Full resource accounting would establish its cost.

milestones.label: A security proof backed by sufficient quantum cost bounds
milestones.explanation: A theorem would have to connect attacks on the complete mechanism to a named lattice problem and prove a sufficient minimum quantum cost. Explicit assumptions and quantitative losses would make the guarantee meaningful.

milestones.label: The proof’s scope and assumptions are explicit
milestones.explanation: The result would have to distinguish assumed difficulty from proved limits and restricted quantum methods from general computation. This would establish exactly which security claim it supports.

milestones.label: Independent researchers can reproduce and check the analysis
milestones.explanation: Published details would have to let independent researchers reproduce cost estimates, check proofs and distinguish ordinary instances from selected examples. This would support scrutiny beyond the original authors.

milestones.label: Consequences are stated separately for each version
milestones.explanation: Results would have to identify which ML-KEM versions they cover and distinguish abstract operation counts from costs on an implemented machine. This would prevent a narrow result from becoming a claim about all lattice cryptography.

uncertain: The proposed attack thresholds lack a consensus justification for practical significance.
The attack and security targets leave room for intermediate outcomes.
Whether a result for the initial target would extend to larger versions or other lattice systems depends on its mathematical mechanism.

page.title: Quantum security classification of ML-KEM
page.definition: ML-KEM lets two parties establish a shared secret over a public channel. A mathematical classification would decide whether ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 meet their respective NIST security categories 1, 3 and 5 against general quantum computation. The question is how much computation it takes to distinguish the shared key from a random key when the adversary can request decapsulation of ciphertexts other than the challenge.

goal.need: In September 2026, hybrid ML-KEM key exchange protected about 70% of browser traffic reaching one web infrastructure provider. Operators protecting data that must stay confidential for years choose parameter sets using estimates of the cost of known attacks. A proof would justify relying on a set at its claimed strength even against undiscovered quantum algorithms. A refutation would identify a set to reconsider for applications requiring that strength. Confidentiality also depends on secure implementation and deployment.

figures.caption: Standardized ML-KEM parameter sets and claimed security categories
figures.note: These are claimed categories, rather than unconditional quantum lower bounds.

statements.quote: The goal of this research is to develop cryptographic algorithms that would be secure against both quantum and classical computers.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology, FIPS 203, section 8
statements.quote:
were designed to meet certain security strength
categories defined by NIST
statements.context: The targets are category 1 for ML-KEM-512, category 3 for ML-KEM-768 and category 5 for ML-KEM-1024. FIPS 203 presents each as a claim.

completion.title: Each ML-KEM parameter set’s NIST category is proved or refuted against general quantum computation.
completion.criterion: For each FIPS 203 set, a peer-reviewed theorem proves or refutes its IND-CCA claim for the specified distributions and functions. Compare with AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256 key search, respectively, at matched success probabilities. State the classical decapsulation-query budget and compare computation, quantum circuit depth and memory under the same resource assumptions. Confirmation requires a lower bound against general quantum computation across the relevant metrics after all reduction losses. Refutation requires a correct attack on that set with a cost below its category benchmark.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis using NIST’s security definitions and category benchmarks; NIST has not prescribed this conclusive-proof test.
completion.basis: NIST defines the benchmarks and makes proofs optional for standardization. Its evaluation permits estimates assuming up to 2^64 chosen ciphertexts and also considers larger query counts. The conclusive theorem is an Atlas criterion. Luo’s preprint was revised on 25 May 2026. A critique of the May claim found that the quantity used for key recovery was unchanged when the secret changed at fixed public matrix. No independently confirmed classification of all three sets was found.

milestones.title: K-PKE has an IND-CPA reduction with two module-LWE terms and one pseudorandom-function term.
milestones.criterion: Bound the chosen-plaintext distinguishing advantage against K-PKE, the encryption scheme inside ML-KEM, by the sum of two module-LWE distinguishing advantages and one pseudorandom-function advantage. The first module-LWE term accounts for the public key and the second for the ciphertext. Model matrix generation as a random oracle and the secret and noise generators as pseudorandom functions. The reduction must hold with classical or quantum access to the random oracle.
milestones.set_by: The field’s IND-CPA security convention; Kyber specification Theorem 1, refined for standardized K-PKE in CRYPTREC Theorem 4.1. The quoted statement was written for Kyber.
milestones.threshold_quote: KYBER.CPAPKE is tightly IND-CPA secure under the Module-LWE hardness assumption.

milestones.title: ML-KEM’s quantum IND-CCA reduction avoids a square-root loss in the base encryption advantage.
milestones.criterion: For a chosen-ciphertext adversary that can query an ideal hash function in superposition, bound its ML-KEM distinguishing advantage by an expression linear in the chosen-plaintext advantage against K-PKE. Give the dependence on the quantum query count, the K-PKE correctness bound and the pseudorandomness of the function used on rejection.
milestones.set_by: Ge, Liao and Xue’s ASIACRYPT 2024 reduction for the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform, specialized to ML-KEM in CRYPTREC Theorem 4.3.
milestones.threshold_quote: Their IND-CCA security can be reduced to the IND-CPA security of the underlying public key encryption (PKE) scheme without the square-root advantage loss.

milestones.title: A concrete quantum reduction leaves ML-KEM’s NIST category conditional only on lattice hardness.
milestones.criterion: For one FIPS 203 parameter set, derive its claimed category from an explicit numerical lower bound on the quantum cost of a named lattice problem. The implication must hold for general quantum circuits, classical chosen-ciphertext access, the specified sampling distributions and the actual symmetric functions. Account for decapsulation failures, resource overhead and probability losses, leaving the stated lattice lower bound as the sole unproved hypothesis.
milestones.set_by: Atlas synthesis from NIST’s category benchmarks and the conditional reductions; no external body’s published milestone requiring this result was found.

milestones.title: ML-KEM has a tight chosen-ciphertext reduction in the classical random-oracle model.
milestones.criterion: For K-PKE with correctness bound δ, let q be the maximum number of classical random-oracle queries. For every ML-KEM chosen-ciphertext adversary, exhibit a K-PKE chosen-plaintext adversary such that the former’s distinguishing advantage is at most three times the latter’s advantage plus (q + 1)δ + q/2^256.
milestones.set_by: The field’s classical random-oracle reduction for the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform, specialized to ML-KEM in CRYPTREC Theorem 4.2.
milestones.threshold_quote:
the IND-CCA security of ML-KEM is tightly bounded by
the IND-CPA security of K-PKE.

not_found: No external body’s published goal or completion criterion for a conclusive quantum classification of all three ML-KEM parameter sets was found.
No externally prescribed sequence extending the existing conditional reductions to an unconditional concrete quantum classification was found.
No independent confirmation or peer-reviewed version of Luo’s claimed ML-KEM quantum attack was found.
No NIST or CRYPTREC statement was found judging a conclusive quantum classification of all three sets infeasible or unnecessary.
